summary: Defines the model and generic mechanisms for encapsulating Internet packets such as IPv4 and IPv6 inside IPv6 packets. This lets traffic cross parts of a network that handle only one kind of packet. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is like putting a letter inside a bigger envelope to send it through a road that only accepts a certain kind of envelope.

subtitle: How to wrap any packet inside an IPv6 packet so it can ride a virtual point-to-point link between two nodes.

tldr.problem: Sometimes a node wants to send selected packets along a particular forwarding path, or carry IPv6 and IPv4 packets across a part of the network, without the nodes in between knowing anything about the original packets.
tldr.mechanism: The entry-point node prepends an IPv6 header (and optional extension headers) to the original packet and sends it to the exit-point node, which strips those headers and forwards the original packet on. The RFC also covers nesting limits, hop limits, packet size and ICMP error relaying.
tldr.outcome: A tunnel behaves like a single-hop virtual link to the packets inside it. RFC 2473 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

Default traffic class and flow label

today: RFC 2473 is a Proposed Standard published in December 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its tunnel model, encapsulation limit option and error relaying rules are therefore still the document of record for generic IPv6 tunneling.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2473 specifies a method and generic mechanisms by which a packet is encapsulated and carried as payload within an IPv6 packet. The result is called an IPv6 tunnel packet, the forwarding path between the source and destination of that packet is an IPv6 tunnel, and the technique is IPv6 tunneling.

A typical scenario is an intermediate node that wants explicit routing control by specifying particular forwarding paths for selected packets. It does this by prepending IPv6 headers to each selected original packet, and those headers identify the path. The RFC describes the generic mechanisms and also the specific cases of tunneling IPv6 and IPv4 packets. Its abstract notes that the model can be applied to other protocol packets as well, such as AppleTalk, IPX or CLNP.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you want a message to take a special road. You put it in an outer envelope addressed to the end of that road, and the road does the rest.

sections.title: The Tunnel Model
sections.content:
An IPv6 tunnel is a virtual link between two IPv6 nodes. To those two nodes it looks like a point-to-point link on which IPv6 acts like a link-layer protocol. The tunnel entry-point node encapsulates original packets and is the source of the tunnel packets. The tunnel exit-point node decapsulates them and is their destination. The packet that gets wrapped is the original packet.

A tunnel is unidirectional: tunnel packets flow one way, from entry-point to exit-point. A bi-directional tunnel is built by configuring two tunnels in opposite directions, so that the entry-point of one is the exit-point of the other. The RFC focuses on tunnels between two unicast addresses, and says the mechanisms also apply when the exit-point is identified by an anycast or multicast address.

An original packet source can be the same node as the entry-point, and the exit-point can be the same node as the final destination.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a one-way road between two houses. If you want traffic both ways, you build a second road going back.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
Encapsulation means prepending an IPv6 header and, optionally, IPv6 extension headers to the original packet. Together these are the tunnel IPv6 headers. The original packet is first processed by the forwarding rules of its own protocol: an IPv6 original packet has its hop limit decremented by one, and an IPv4 original packet has its time to live decremented by one. The tunnel header's source field is then filled with an address of the entry-point node, the destination with an address of the exit-point, and the packet is sent toward the exit-point.

Nodes inside the tunnel treat the tunnel packet as an ordinary IPv6 packet. For example, a Hop-by-Hop Options header is processed by each receiving node, a Routing header steers the path, and a Destination Options header is processed at the exit-point.

Decapsulation happens when the exit-point receives an IPv6 packet addressed to it. It applies the strict left-to-right extension header rules, and when the Next Header value in the last header processed is a tunnel protocol value, the tunnel protocol engine discards the tunnel headers and hands the original packet to the protocol that value names. If Next Header is the IPv6 tunnel protocol value, the original packet goes back to the IPv6 layer.

The RFC also describes an IPv6 tunnel protocol engine that behaves as both an upper-layer protocol (taking in tunnel packets to decapsulate) and a link layer (taking in original packets to encapsulate). A tunnel is selected over other links by the node's routing table.
sections.eli5: The entry house puts your letter in a big envelope and mails it. The exit house opens the big envelope, throws it away, and delivers the letter inside.

sections.title: The Tunnel IPv6 Header
sections.content:
The entry-point fills in the tunnel IPv6 main header like this. Version is 6. Traffic Class is either copied from the original packet or set to a pre-configured value. Flow Label is a pre-configured value, typically zero. Payload Length is the original packet length plus the length of any prepended extension headers.

Next Header follows the normal IPv6 assignments. For an IPv6 original packet it is decimal 41 when there are no tunnel extension headers, 0 if a Hop-by-Hop Options header comes next, or 60 if a Destination Options header comes next. Hop Limit is a pre-configured value (see the state variables). Source Address is the configured entry-point address and Destination Address is the configured exit-point address.

Depending on configuration, the entry-point may also add extension headers such as a Hop-by-Hop Options or Routing header. If it is configured to limit nesting, it adds a Destination Options header carrying the Tunnel Encapsulation Limit option, described next.
sections.eli5: The big envelope needs its own address label. It says who is sending it, where it is going, and what kind of thing is inside.

sections.title: Nested Tunnels and the Encapsulation Limit
sections.content:
Nested encapsulation happens when a hop of a tunnel is itself a tunnel: the outer tunnel contains an inner tunnel, and the inner entry-point treats the outer tunnel's packets as original packets and wraps them again. Each wrap adds a header, so the packet grows and may need fragmentation. The RFC notes that fragmenting an already fragmented tunnel packet doubles the number of fragments, so it recommends limiting nesting.

The mechanism is the Tunnel Encapsulation Limit option, carried in a Destination Options header placed between the encapsulating IPv6 header and the original packet's header. It is an 8-bit unsigned value saying how many further levels of encapsulation are allowed, not counting the one holding the option. The option type is decimal 4, the data length is 1, and a limit of zero means the packet may not enter another tunnel before leaving this one.

Every entry-point MUST examine packets entering the tunnel. If the option is present with value zero, the packet is discarded and an ICMP Parameter Problem message goes to the previous entry-point. If it is present and non-zero, the new encapsulation includes the option with the value reduced by one. If it is absent and a limit is configured, the option is added with the configured limit. If it is absent and no limit is configured, none is added. The option is removed at the tunnel's exit-point.

Two cases to avoid are loopback encapsulation, where an entry-point encapsulates packets from itself to itself and could loop forever, and routing-loop nested encapsulation, where packets re-enter an outer tunnel they have not yet left. Because each nested wrap gets a fresh hop limit, the hop limit alone cannot stop that, so the RFC says to control both the original packet hop limit and the encapsulation limit. Appendix A explains that the risk is lowest for routes to a single node, medium for routes to a prefix, and highest for a default route.
sections.eli5: If you keep putting envelopes inside envelopes, the pile gets huge. So each envelope carries a counter saying how many more envelopes may be added, and when it hits zero, no more.

sections.title: Tunnel State Variables
sections.content:
Several settings live on the entry-point node. The entry and exit addresses must be valid IPv6 unicast addresses of the nodes, and their configuration is not subject to autoconfiguration or Neighbor Discovery.

The tunnel hop limit models the tunnel as a single-hop virtual link: the entry-point sets the tunnel header's hop limit independently of the original header, which hides the tunnel's internal hop count from the original packet. It should be high enough to reach the exit-point yet low enough that a routing loop inside the tunnel expires quickly. The default for hosts is the Neighbor Discovery advertised hop limit, and for routers the default IPv6 Hop Limit from Assigned Numbers (64 at the time of writing).

The traffic class default is zero and can be copied from the original header or set to a configured value. The flow label default is zero. The recommended default for the encapsulation limit is 4. The tunnel MTU is set dynamically to the Path MTU between the entry and exit points minus the size of the tunnel headers, using Path MTU discovery, and the tunnel MTU of a nested tunnel is the outer tunnel's MTU minus the nested headers.
sections.eli5: The entry house keeps a settings sheet: where the road starts and ends, how many stops the big envelope may make, and how big a parcel fits.

sections.title: Packet Size and Error Reporting
sections.content:
Prepending a header makes packets bigger. The tunnel packet counts as a packet originating at the entry-point, so the entry-point must support fragmentation, while intermediate nodes must not fragment. The exit-point reassembles fragments before looking for an embedded packet. If the original packet exceeds the tunnel MTU, an IPv6 original larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU is discarded and an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message goes back, while a smaller one is encapsulated and then fragmented. For IPv4, a packet with the Don't Fragment bit set is discarded with an unreachable, packet too big reply, and one without it is encapsulated and fragmented.

For errors, IPv6 tunneling follows the general rule that an ICMP message goes to the packet's source. An error inside a tunnel goes to the tunnel entry-point, which must relay it to the source of the original packet. The tunnel problems that get relayed are hop limit exceeded, unreachable node, parameter problem (the encapsulation limit was exceeded) and packet too big. The first three are reported to the original source as a generic unreachable caused by a link problem. For nested tunnels, the inner entry-point relays to the outer entry-point, which relays to the original source.
sections.eli5: If the parcel is too big for the road, it gets cut into pieces or sent back with a note. If something breaks on the road, the report goes to the entry house, which tells the original sender.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An IPv6 tunnel can be secured by securing the IPv6 path between the entry-point and exit-point, using the IP security architecture and the Authentication Header (AH) or Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). A secure tunnel can act as a gateway-to-gateway secure path. The entry-point adds the security headers as part of the tunnel headers, and the exit-point processes and then discards them.

How much integrity, authentication and confidentiality a tunnel gets depends on whether AH or ESP is used and on the Security Association. The RFC says there is no dependency between the security applied to tunnel packets and the security applied to the original packets inside, and each inner tunnel in a nest may have its own security services.
sections.eli5: You can put a lock on the big envelope. That lock is separate from any lock on the letter inside.
